location.basis: Centre of our z18 mosaic, placed after locating the site on the Esri imagery from its published position (OpenStreetMap point via Pleiades, 27.3217 N, 68.1366 E) and identifying the citadel by the Buddhist stupa (27.32541 N, 68.13344 E) and the excavated lower-town blocks east of it. The measured lines lie between 27.3216 and 27.3271 N, 68.1325 and 68.1375 E.

main_system_reason: sys1 is the orthogonal grid of house walls and lanes that we measured in all three excavated lower-town blocks; it carries the most lines and the greatest measured length, and the lines from the three blocks agree within about two degrees. The street edges of sys2 belong to the same lower town but run several degrees clockwise of the house walls that line them, so we report them separately rather than as the town's axis.
notes: The Esri imagery here is a Vantor Vivid mosaic with real detail only to zoom 18 (zoom 19 returns the grey 'map data not yet available' tile), so we measured at 0.53 m per pixel. Brick walls about one metre thick appear two pixels wide, and the clearest edges are the dark shadow bands that walls cast towards the north-west. The exposed architecture lies in four places: the citadel mound with the Buddhist stupa and its square monastery, the excavated buildings west of the stupa and the L area further south on the same mound, and three excavated blocks of the lower town east of the citadel. We left out the stupa and the monastery cells around it because they are Kushan-period construction, and we also left out the diagonal paths and fences of the visitor circuit and an inclined dark band in the citadel that looks like a trench or mound edge. Many walls inside the dense house blocks break into short segments at this resolution; we kept only lines that stayed continuous on the rectified strip, so the lower-town house system rests on eight lines and several candidate lines were rejected after inspection. The street edges (NB5, MB1, SB1) are lines of house fronts that step progressively along the street; they turn several degrees clockwise of the walls of the houses themselves, and we report them as a separate system. The L area on the southern part of the citadel is visibly turned clockwise against the rest of the site; its walls are short (12 to 23 m) and partly eroded, so its system has a large spread, but the rotation is plain on the image. Area names in brackets (DK-G, HR, VS, L) are our identification from the position of the blocks and are not read from a plan.
